justification: run-code is green three separate times (blocks=25, executed=12), including the timed List<T>-vs-Queue<T> comparison and the n-up-to-10,000 amortized push/pop count, with no flakiness. I hand-traced the RingQueue<T> sequence in the article (capacity 4; enqueue A,B,C,D; dequeue twice; enqueue E,F,G) against the exact Enqueue/Dequeue/Grow code shown, slot by slot: head=2,count=2 -> tail=(2+2)%4=0 puts E at slot 0 (physically before head, matching Figure 2); F lands at slot 1; the final Enqueue(G) triggers Grow, which copies items[(head+i)%4] for i=0..3 into an 8-slot array (C,D,E,F) and resets head=0, then writes G at slot 4 -> 'C D E F G . . .  h=0 cap=8'. This is exactly what the article prints; the trace is genuine, not fabricated or rounded to look clean. I separately traced the find-the-bug exercise (BrokenRingQueue, capacity 4, no _count): after four enqueues _tail wraps to 0 = _head, so IsEmpty reports true on a full buffer; Enqueue(5) overwrites slot 0 (value 1, never read); the drain loop reads only '5' before head==tail again, silently losing 2, 3 and 4. This matches the article's shown output and is a real, demonstrable data-loss bug, not a hand-waved one. I fetched the live dotnet/runtime source directly (raw.githubusercontent.com, main branch) for both files. Stack.cs: DefaultCapacity = 4, Push falls through to PushWithResize -> Grow(capacity) when size == _array.Length, newcapacity = 2 * _array.Length (exact doubling) -- confirms the article's Capacity trace (4, 4, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, 16) exactly. Queue.cs: fields _array/_head/_tail/_size match; MoveNext is verbatim 'int tmp = index + 1; if (tmp == _array.Length) tmp = 0; index = tmp;' -- an exact match to the block quoted in the article, including the real source's own comment that % is slower than the branch, which the article paraphrases accurately; Grow uses GrowFactor=2, MinimumGrow=4, confirming the article's claim that Queue<T> grows the same way but keeps Capacity flat across a dequeue/enqueue cycle because SetCapacity only fires when size==array.Length. I also fetched Stack<T>'s and Queue<T>'s Microsoft Learn pages directly and confirmed the exact quoted sentences ('Stack<T> is implemented as an array' / 'this class implements a generic queue as a circular array'), and List<T>.RemoveAt's page, which states verbatim 'This method is an O(n) operation, where n is (Count - index)', matching the article's citation precisely. I fetched the live System.Collections.Generic namespace page (default moniker net-11.0-pp, updated 2026-05-27): no Deque<T> is listed among the Classes; the article's 'no public Deque<T>' claim is accurate and current, not stale. However, I found one genuine, demonstrable factual error, which under the rubric caps this score: the article attributes a direct quotation to cp-algorithms.com -- '"maintain[ing] a deque in a state, where they are monotonically increasing (or decreasing)"' -- to the exact page cited in front matter (stack_queue_modification.html). I fetched that page's live HTML directly (not just a summarized read) and grepped the raw markup: the word 'monoton' does not appear anywhere on the page, the phrase 'deque in a state' does not appear anywhere on the page, and the only two occurrences of 'deque' on the page are inside C++ code (`deque<int>`, `deque<pair<...>>`). The page (titled 'Minimum Stack / Minimum Queue') does describe a related idea in different words -- 'we will keep the queue in nondecreasing order' -- but the article's bracketed, quotation-marked sentence is not that sentence and is not on the page at all. This is a fabricated quotation attributed to a real, cited primary source, which is exactly the failure mode CLAUDE.md's binding rules and the editorial brief's hard rule 1 ('nothing fabricated... no invented quotes') exist to catch; it is worse than an ordinary factual slip because it invents words and puts them in a real source's mouth. I also note the Sedgewick & Wayne / algs4 source is listed in front matter and accessed, but is never cited inline anywhere in the article body -- a second, minor instance of the brief's binding lesson ('a source in the list that is never cited inline... is a finding'). Against comparable published material: GeeksforGeeks's circular-queue page is fixed-capacity only, gives no step-by-step wraparound trace and no growth/amortized discussion at all; Sedgewick & Wayne's own section 1.3 covers resizing-array and linked-list implementations at a similar rigor but with no measured timing and no live-runtime-source verification. The real-measured-timing (List<T> vs Queue<T>, wildcarded panel plus one real run's table), the real hand-traceable RingQueue<T> wraparound, and the direct dotnet/runtime source fetch-and-verify (down to exact field names and growth constants) are a genuine differentiator over both comparison sources and would, on their own, be 9+ territory. The fabricated cp-algorithms quotation is the one thing that pulls it back down.

issues.location: 'A next-greater-element with a monotonic stack', second paragraph: 'cp-algorithms describes the same idea for a minimum-tracking structure, "maintain[ing] a deque in a state, where they are monotonically increasing (or decreasing)" by removing disqualified elements before adding a new one.'
issues.problem: This is presented as a direct quotation (quotation marks plus a bracketed grammatical edit, '[ing]') from the cited source, https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/stack_queue_modification.html. I fetched the live page and grepped its raw HTML: the word 'monoton' (in any form) does not appear anywhere on the page, and the phrase 'deque in a state' does not appear anywhere on the page. The only two uses of the substring 'deque' on the page are C++ code (`deque<int>`, `deque<pair<int,int>>`). The page (titled 'Minimum Stack / Minimum Queue') expresses a related idea differently: 'we will keep the queue in nondecreasing order (i.e. the smallest value will be stored in the head)'. The quoted sentence is fabricated -- invented text attributed to a real, cited primary source that does not contain it. This is a hard-rule violation ('nothing fabricated... no invented quotes') and a demonstrable factual error, which caps the technical score.
issues.fixLooksLike: Remove the quotation marks and bracketed edit. Either paraphrase the page's real idea in the writer's own words with no quotation marks ('cp-algorithms describes the same idea for a minimum-tracking queue: keep it in nondecreasing order by removing any trailing elements the new value disqualifies before adding it'), or quote the page's actual sentence verbatim if a direct quote is wanted ('the queue in nondecreasing order (i.e. the smallest value will be stored in the head)').

issues.location: 'One end only: array-backed or linked': 'General-purpose libraries mostly pick the array, because a doubling pause that happens once every few thousand pushes on average costs less overall than an allocation on every single one.'
issues.problem: This is a reasonable, well-hedged generalization ('mostly'), but it is asserted with no source and no comparison point (e.g. Java's ArrayDeque vs LinkedList, or an explicit contrast with .NET's own LinkedList<T>). It reads as a claim a strong student would want backed by at least one concrete counter-example or citation, given the brief's binding lesson that generalisations get checked.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either cite a source for the general design trend (e.g. Sedgewick & Wayne's discussion of resizing-array vs linked-list stacks, which is already in the source list but uncited -- see the issue above) or scope the claim more tightly to .NET specifically, since that is the only case actually demonstrated on the page.
